clusters.title: ET Wealth Expo: Saurabh Mukherjea suggests a simple 50:50 portfolio to diversify across India and the US
clusters.description: A simple way to build a diversified portfolio, according to Saurabh Mukherjea, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of Marcellus Investment Managers, is to split investments equally between the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500 and rebalance annually.Speaking at ET Wealth Expo in Mumbai on Saturday, Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict which market will perform better in the coming years. Instead, they can invest equally in the Indian and US markets and rebalance their portfolios once a year to maintain the 50:50 allocation.He said investors can choose a fixed date for rebalancing, such as their birthday or February 1, the Budget day, and bring their portfolio back to the 50:50 allocation on that date every year.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: US stocks epitomise anti-asset allocation; international debt better option: S Naren, ICICI…

primary.title: ET Wealth Expo: Saurabh Mukherjea suggests a simple 50:50 portfolio to diversify across India and the US
primary.description: A simple way to build a diversified portfolio, according to Saurabh Mukherjea, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of Marcellus Investment Managers, is to split investments equally between the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500 and rebalance annually.Speaking at ET Wealth Expo in Mumbai on Saturday, Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict which market will perform better in the coming years. Instead, they can invest equally in the Indian and US markets and rebalance their portfolios once a year to maintain the 50:50 allocation.He said investors can choose a fixed date for rebalancing, such as their birthday or February 1, the Budget day, and bring their portfolio back to the 50:50 allocation on that date every year.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: US stocks epitomise anti-asset allocation; international debt better option: S Naren, ICICI Prudential MFAccording to Mukherjea, this is the simplest, lowest-cost and cheapest diversified portfolio, based on the asset allocation theory of Harry Markowitz, who received the Nobel Prize in 1990 and developed the theory in 1952. Mukherjea explained three benefits of following this approach.The first benefit is that the portfolio's returns can move towards the higher-returning asset rather than remaining at the mathematical average of the returns generated by the two assets.Mukherjea explained that when investors allocate money to two diversified assets that have little relationship with each other and rebalance annually, the returns can move towards the higher of the two assets over time.He clarified that diversification does not mean investing in five Indian mutual funds, five small-cap funds or five domestic portfolio management services (PMS). It means investing in two assets that have little relationship with each other.The second benefit is lower volatility. According to Mukherjea, the portfolio's volatility can move towards the lower of the two assets rather than remaining at their mathematical average. This means investors can potentially get higher returns while experiencing lower volatility. As a result, the return-to-risk ratio of the portfolio improves.He described this as the free lunch of finance because investors can increase returns while reducing portfolio risk through diversification.The third benefit is that investors do not need to forecast which market will perform better. Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict whether India or the US will outperform over the next 10 years. They also do not need to worry about political developments, government decisions, budgets or changes in long-term capital gains tax to follow this allocation strategy.By maintaining a 50:50 allocation and rebalancing once a year, investors can benefit from whichever market performs better.Explaining the rebalancing mechanism, Mukherjea said investors should start with an equal allocation to the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo | India is still in SIP accumulation phase; SWPs may gain relevance in 25 years: Vikas KhemaniHe added that, over time, if one market performs better, its share in the portfolio will increase. At the time of annual rebalancing, investors sell some of the investment in the market that has become more expensive and invest more in the market that has become cheaper to bring the allocation back to 50:50.The market expert explained that this process involves buying more of the cheaper market and selling the more expensive market.Responding to a question from the audience about why the portfolio's return would not immediately become the mathematical average of the two markets, Mukherjea said the effect of rebalancing becomes more evident over a longer period.He said that if investors continue the 50:50 allocation and annual rebalancing for another 10 years, the returns would move closer to the higher-returning asset. Similarly, the portfolio's volatility would move closer to the lower-volatility asset.According to him, the longer investors continue this process, the less relevant the lower-returning asset becomes in determining the portfolio's returns and volatility. Mukherjea also highlighted the importance of global investing, pointing out that a large part of Indian investors' expenses is linked to foreign markets.Mukherjea mentioned that around 70% of day-to-day expenses are effectively in dollars, even though people believe they are spending in Indian rupees. He cited overseas education, foreign holidays, electronics, medicines, watches, aviation fuel and other imported products as examples.He said Indian families spend around $9 billion annually on overseas education, while approximately 33 million Indians travel abroad on holidays every year. Assuming an expenditure of $1,000 per person, this amounts to around $30 billion in foreign holiday spending.He also referred to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), under which around $35 billion goes abroad every year.According to Mukherjea, investors should consider global investing because their expenses and aspirations are increasingly linked to the global economy. He also pointed out that India accounts for around 3% of the global market, making global markets significantly larger than the domestic market.However, he cautioned investors that global investing requires care because they are exposed to tax regimes in other countries. He also highlighted the scale of global markets and said investors should not treat global investing as an opportunity to casually trade through a brokerage account.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: In uncertain markets, investors can control only consistency and quality of their inputs, says Swarup Mohanty, Mirae Asset MFHe said investors should understand the tax implications and the wider range of investment opportunities available globally.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)If you have any mutual fund queries, message on ET Mutual Funds on Facebook/Twitter. We will get it answered by our panel of experts. primary.title: Sebi pushes for resilient capital markets, focuses on investor protection: Chairman
primary.description: SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Saturday said the regulator is continuously working to make the country's capital markets more accessible, efficient and resilient, with a core approach focused on facilitating capital formation, improving ease of doing business and strengthening investors' protection.Speaking on capital market expansion at the Bharat Chamber of Commerce Investors Forum here, Pandey noted that the market capitalisation has grown strongly over the past decade, with companies raising on average more than Rs 10 lakh crore annually through equity and debt issuances."While we continue to strengthen markets for businesses, an equally important priority is investor protection. World-class markets must be not only efficient during normal times, but also resilient during periods of stress," he said."Our approach has been to facilitate capital formation, improve ease of doing business, and strengthen investor protection," Pandey said, highlighting that these objectives reinforce each other.Focusing on regional growth, the SEBI chairman pointed out that participation from West Bengal has expanded considerably, with the number of investors in the securities market increasing from around 12 lakh in the 2015 financial year to over 90 lakh today, approximately 36 per cent of whom are young investors below 30 years of age.Additionally, 379 listed companies have registered offices in West Bengal, and over 40 MSMEs from the state have accessed capital markets to raise over Rs 1,400 crore through SME IPOs.To reduce unnecessary compliance burdens and improve operational efficiency, Pandey said the Securities and Exchange Board of India has taken several steps to make fundraising simpler and more cost-effective.These include streamlining IPO processes, shortening timelines for rights issues, rationalising listing requirements for large issuers, permitting certain employee stock options after listing under prescribed conditions, reducing listing timelines for public issues, enabling debt securities with lower face values, and relaxing mandatory merchant banking requirements for eligible issuers undertaking private placements.On the investor front, Pandey emphasised that financial education and protection remain paramount, noting that an informed investor serves as the first line of defence."Building world-class capital markets is not merely about achieving higher market capitalisation, larger trading volumes, or faster transactions. The real measure is how effectively markets connect savings with productive investment, support businesses in raising capital, and create opportunities for investors to participate in economic growth."

primary.title: Hardeep Puri files nomination for MP bypolls
primary.description: Bhopal: Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Saturday filed his nomination for the upcoming Rajya Sabha by-election from Madhya Pradesh.Earlier, Puri visited the Karunadham Ashram in Bhopal.The BJP Central Election Committee on Wednesday announced the nomination of Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri as the party's candidate for the upcoming Rajya Sabha by-election from Madhya Pradesh.According to an official press release issued from the BJP central office at Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, the Central Election Committee gave its approval to Puri's candidature for the upper house seat representing the state."The Central Election Committee of the Bharatiya Janata Party has given its approval to the name for the upcoming Rajya Sabha by-election 2026 in Madhya Pradesh: Hardeep Singh Puri," the party statement read.The announcement comes as preparations are underway for the lone Rajya Sabha seat from Madhya Pradesh, which fell vacant following the resignation of former Union Minister L. Murugan.Earlier on October 22, the Election Commission of India (ECI) announced the schedule for the upcoming by-election to the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) from Madhya Pradesh, following the resignation of Murugan.According to a press note issued by the ECI, the vacancy arose on October 14, 2026, following Murugan's resignation. His term in the Upper House was originally slated to conclude on April 2, 2030.According to the official schedule, the notification for the by-poll will be issued on October 26, 2026.The last date for filing nominations is November 2, 2026, with scrutiny scheduled for November 3, 2026. The last date for the withdrawal of candidatures has been fixed as November 5, 2026.Voting will take place on November 12, between 9:00 AM and 4:00 PM, followed by the counting of votes on the same day at 5:00 PM.The entire election process is scheduled to be completed before November 16, the poll panel stated.Puri, a veteran diplomat-turned-politician, currently serves as a Union Cabinet Minister in the central government.

mutual_fund_news.title: ET Wealth Expo: Saurabh Mukherjea suggests a simple 50:50 portfolio to diversify across India and the US
mutual_fund_news.description: A simple way to build a diversified portfolio, according to Saurabh Mukherjea, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of Marcellus Investment Managers, is to split investments equally between the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500 and rebalance annually.Speaking at ET Wealth Expo in Mumbai on Saturday, Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict which market will perform better in the coming years. Instead, they can invest equally in the Indian and US markets and rebalance their portfolios once a year to maintain the 50:50 allocation.He said investors can choose a fixed date for rebalancing, such as their birthday or February 1, the Budget day, and bring their portfolio back to the 50:50 allocation on that date every year.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: US stocks epitomise anti-asset allocation; international debt better option: S Naren, ICICI…

primary.title: ET Wealth Expo: Saurabh Mukherjea suggests a simple 50:50 portfolio to diversify across India and the US
primary.description: A simple way to build a diversified portfolio, according to Saurabh Mukherjea, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of Marcellus Investment Managers, is to split investments equally between the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500 and rebalance annually.Speaking at ET Wealth Expo in Mumbai on Saturday, Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict which market will perform better in the coming years. Instead, they can invest equally in the Indian and US markets and rebalance their portfolios once a year to maintain the 50:50 allocation.He said investors can choose a fixed date for rebalancing, such as their birthday or February 1, the Budget day, and bring their portfolio back to the 50:50 allocation on that date every year.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: US stocks epitomise anti-asset allocation; international debt better option: S Naren, ICICI Prudential MFAccording to Mukherjea, this is the simplest, lowest-cost and cheapest diversified portfolio, based on the asset allocation theory of Harry Markowitz, who received the Nobel Prize in 1990 and developed the theory in 1952. Mukherjea explained three benefits of following this approach.The first benefit is that the portfolio's returns can move towards the higher-returning asset rather than remaining at the mathematical average of the returns generated by the two assets.Mukherjea explained that when investors allocate money to two diversified assets that have little relationship with each other and rebalance annually, the returns can move towards the higher of the two assets over time.He clarified that diversification does not mean investing in five Indian mutual funds, five small-cap funds or five domestic portfolio management services (PMS). It means investing in two assets that have little relationship with each other.The second benefit is lower volatility. According to Mukherjea, the portfolio's volatility can move towards the lower of the two assets rather than remaining at their mathematical average. This means investors can potentially get higher returns while experiencing lower volatility. As a result, the return-to-risk ratio of the portfolio improves.He described this as the free lunch of finance because investors can increase returns while reducing portfolio risk through diversification.The third benefit is that investors do not need to forecast which market will perform better. Mukherjea said investors do not need to predict whether India or the US will outperform over the next 10 years. They also do not need to worry about political developments, government decisions, budgets or changes in long-term capital gains tax to follow this allocation strategy.By maintaining a 50:50 allocation and rebalancing once a year, investors can benefit from whichever market performs better.Explaining the rebalancing mechanism, Mukherjea said investors should start with an equal allocation to the Nifty 50 and the S&P 500.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo | India is still in SIP accumulation phase; SWPs may gain relevance in 25 years: Vikas KhemaniHe added that, over time, if one market performs better, its share in the portfolio will increase. At the time of annual rebalancing, investors sell some of the investment in the market that has become more expensive and invest more in the market that has become cheaper to bring the allocation back to 50:50.The market expert explained that this process involves buying more of the cheaper market and selling the more expensive market.Responding to a question from the audience about why the portfolio's return would not immediately become the mathematical average of the two markets, Mukherjea said the effect of rebalancing becomes more evident over a longer period.He said that if investors continue the 50:50 allocation and annual rebalancing for another 10 years, the returns would move closer to the higher-returning asset. Similarly, the portfolio's volatility would move closer to the lower-volatility asset.According to him, the longer investors continue this process, the less relevant the lower-returning asset becomes in determining the portfolio's returns and volatility. Mukherjea also highlighted the importance of global investing, pointing out that a large part of Indian investors' expenses is linked to foreign markets.Mukherjea mentioned that around 70% of day-to-day expenses are effectively in dollars, even though people believe they are spending in Indian rupees. He cited overseas education, foreign holidays, electronics, medicines, watches, aviation fuel and other imported products as examples.He said Indian families spend around $9 billion annually on overseas education, while approximately 33 million Indians travel abroad on holidays every year. Assuming an expenditure of $1,000 per person, this amounts to around $30 billion in foreign holiday spending.He also referred to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), under which around $35 billion goes abroad every year.According to Mukherjea, investors should consider global investing because their expenses and aspirations are increasingly linked to the global economy. He also pointed out that India accounts for around 3% of the global market, making global markets significantly larger than the domestic market.However, he cautioned investors that global investing requires care because they are exposed to tax regimes in other countries. He also highlighted the scale of global markets and said investors should not treat global investing as an opportunity to casually trade through a brokerage account.Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: In uncertain markets, investors can control only consistency and quality of their inputs, says Swarup Mohanty, Mirae Asset MFHe said investors should understand the tax implications and the wider range of investment opportunities available globally.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own.
